newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks burst higher as jobs report pleases.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks burst higher as jobs report pleases.

text.p: Wall Street stocks blazed higher on Friday, propelled by fresh evidence that the U.S. economy was enjoying robust growth with low inflation.

The Dow industrials surged 83 points to close unofficially at 6856, just 27 points shy of their all-time closing high. The S&P 500 index and New York Stock Exchange Composite index both ended at unofficial record highs.
Sparking the rally was a monthly employment report that showed stronger-than-expected U.S. job growth but tame wage increases. The data muted concern about wage-driven inflation.
Analysts keyed on the fact that wage growth was barely perceptible in January, with the average hourly wage rising to $12.06 from $12.05.
The tame inflation implications of the report sent bonds higher and stocks quickly followed suit. The Dow industrials surged 95 points in the first hour of trading.
"The market got what it wanted, particularly from the hourly earnings number, which was very encouraging on inflation," said Guy Truicko, portfolio manager at Unity Management.

The surge in share prices in the first hour of trading, just after the data was released, suggested to analysts that some of January's mutual fund inflows have been held on the sidelines, awaiting a signal to enter the market.
"What I see is a lot of cash waiting in the background," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities. "Every time we've seen good news, the market has shot up."
To be sure, with every step higher, the market has also exhibited increasing wariness.
That skittishness was apparent during the session's frenzied afternoon, when comments about the dollar by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin send markets gyrating.

Rubin, speaking in Washington ahead of a meeting of the Group of Seven nations in Berlin, said a strong dollar remained in the U.S. interest but he expected foreign exchange issues would be a key topic at the weekend G-7 meeting.

Rubin's remark -- a less vigorous endorsement of the dollar than currency markets had grown accustomed -- provoked a sharp dollar sell-off that spilled over into bonds and stocks, dragging the Dow briefly into negative territory.

"One of the bullish props, particularly for bonds, was the strong dollar," said Anthony O'Bryan, market analyst at A.G. Edwards. "When the dollar gave back gains, that hit bonds and triggered futures-related sell programs."
As bonds recovered, however, programs quickly ensued on the buy side, producing a choppy finish that saw the Dow ultimately surge nearly all the way back to its morning peak.
Financial stocks were broadly higher, benefiting from the improved interest rate climate. Citicorp jumped 4-1/8 to 120-3/4 and BankAmerica Corp rose 3-5/8 to 118-7/8.
American Express Corp gained 3-3/8 to 65-3/8 after news that U.S. Justice Department staff attorneys were considering an antitrust suit against Visa and MasterCard.
The suit, if filed, would challenge Visa and MasterCard's practice of prohibiting their U.S. member banks from issuing American Express cards.
Drugstore chain Revco D.S. Inc climbed 3-3/8 to 41-3/8 after agreeing to a $2.8 billion stock acquisition by CVS Corp. CVS shares rose 3-1/8 to 47-1/8.
Physician Support Systems Inc plunged 9-1/16 to 7-1/2 after warning of disappointing fourth-quarter earnings. Cowen & Co downgraded the shares to buy from strong buy after the warning.
America Online Inc fell 2-1/4 to 35-7/8. The company reported a second-quarter loss late Thursday. Several Wall Street firms later cut their ratings on the shares.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 11.31 to 1357.71.
The S&P 500 index rose 9.41 to 789.56, a record.
The Russell 2000 index of small-cap stocks rose 1.27 to 366.75.
For the week, the Dow rose 42.71 points.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
